action.description: Action object MUST contain a field `submission`, and MAY contain arbitrary additional information.

actTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) to obtain an action from an agent.

episodeSteps.description: Maximum number of steps in the episode.

includeLegalActions.description: If true, include legalActions and legalActionStrings in observations. Defaults to false since these can be derived from serializedGameAndState.

initialActions.description: Actions applied to initial state before play begins to set up starting position.

loadPresetHands.description: Repeated poker only. Load preset hand chance actions from preset_hands.jsonl.

openSpielGameName.description: The short_name of the OpenSpiel game to load.

openSpielGameParameters.description: Game parameters for Open Spiel game.

openSpielGameString.description: The full game string including parameters.

presetHands.description: Repeated poker only. List of per-hand chance action sequences to use instead of random chance.

runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.status: OK; Setup step; model not called.

info.agentSelfReportedStatus: OK; Setup step; model not called.

action.thoughts:
The current game state shows a standard 6x7 Connect 4 board. Player 'x' has made the first move by placing a piece in the bottom-most cell of column 3 (the center column). As player 'o', the optimal strategy in Connect 4 is to control the center.

Column 3 is the most versatile column, as it is involved in the highest number of potential winning combinations: vertical, horizontal, and diagonal. By playing in column 3, you achieve two things:
1. You block player 'x' from potentially building a vertical line in that column.
2. You establish your own presence in the center, which is crucial for both offensive and defensive play.

Standard Connect 4 opening theory and computer-based solvers indicate that the best responses for the second player to an opening in the center column are to play in column 2, 3, or 4. Among these, playing in column 3 (stacking directly on top of the opponent's piece) is a very strong and common move that effectively neutralizes the center and delays any potential advantage for the first player. Given the empty board otherwise, column 3 is a solid and optimal choice.

Final Answer: 3

No immediate threats exist for either player, as neither has even two connected pieces yet, and no column is close to being full. All columns 0-6 are legal moves.

In Connect 4 strategy, the center column is powerful, but playing there now would drop a new x piece at row 3 (directly above o). This creates no direct connection to the existing x at row 5 (the o blocks adjacency), limiting immediate horizontal, vertical, or diagonal potential from the new piece. Instead, the optimal approach is to build directly adjacent to the existing x piece at the bottom. Column 2 achieves this without overcommitting to the blocked center. (Column 4 is symmetrically equivalent and also strong.) This follows standard opening principles for this position after x3-o3, prioritizing connectivity and central control while forcing o to respond defensively rather than building their own threats.

The current board state has X pieces at (row 5, col 2) and (row 5, col 3), with O pieces at (row 4, col 3) and (row 3, col 3). No player has 3 or more consecutive pieces in any direction, so neither can win on the immediate next turn (X will have 3 pieces total after this move; O will have 3).

Dropping an X into column 4 causes it to land at (row 5, col 4). This creates three consecutive X pieces along row 5 at columns 2-4. This position creates an immediate double threat: on the subsequent turn, X can win by dropping into column 1 (forming columns 1-4 horizontal) or column 5 (forming columns 2-5 horizontal). O can respond with only one move and thus can block at most one of these columns. X will then complete the unblocked line of 4 on the turn after that.

No other column creates a comparable forcing position this quickly. For example:
- Column 1 creates a symmetric double threat (and is also winning), but column 4 is more central.
- Columns such as 2 or 3 create no line of 3 and thus no immediate forcing threats, allowing O to potentially develop their own lines (e.g., extending vertically in column 3).

This forces a win for X regardless of O's responses.

Final Answer: 4
